title: The Lopsided Pot of Truth
markdown:
Once upon a time, Willow Creek was so small the welcome sign was really just a friendly wave from Mrs. Higgins next door, who also happened to be the town gossip. The history, as advertised, was another matter. Mayor Tibbs had cooked up a past more spectacular than a circus tent, and he served it hot.

Every day a travelling saleswoman named Elise Porter zipped through like a hummingbird with a sparkly suitcase. She arrived with a cheerful ta-da and unpacked her wares: wooden ducks that supposedly quacked prophecies (they squeaked, but with conviction), knitted socks that guaranteed you would never stub your toe (they were simply very comfortable, but shh). Her method was a dash of sparkle, a heap of imagination, and a generous sprinkle of oh, this is ancient, practically from a pharaoh's sock drawer. She called it historical embellishment. Artistic licence for the sake of a yarn. The suitcase was always nearly full.

Every day, too, Mayor Bartholomew Tibbs polished Willow Creek's past until it gleamed brighter than a new penny. He strutted, a monocle perched as if officialdom were a hobby, proclaiming that this very cobblestone — worn by time and, ah, scurrying mice — had been trod by the legendary Gurgle-Gurgle the Great, who invented looking incredibly important while holding a very large turnip. Tourists ooh'd, mostly at the gall. He was a showman. The town, which liked him, let the turnip stand.

Until one day Elise, on a quest for antique buttons, rummaged in an abandoned shed so forgotten its cobwebs might have paid rates. She expected a dusty sewing machine, or a very sleepy spider. She tripped. Crash. A small lumpy surprisingly heavy object tumbled from under sacks that smelled of old cheese. A lopsided, very old clay pot. She brushed off the dust. Her sales-brain whirred. Could this be the Goblet of Giggles? The Chalice of Chuckles?

Because of that, Mayor Tibbs, who had a nose for any attraction that could be spun into gold, swooped in faster than a greased ferret. "Eureka! This, my dear Elise, is no mere goblet. This is the ancient Willow Creek Vessel of Vitality. It once held the tears of a mythical river sprite, which, when sprinkled upon the land, grant eternal — uh — good cheer and perfect hair days!"

The pot felt old in a way ducks and socks did not. The sprite part was Tibbs-fluff, substance zero. This was real, and she had found it, and her stomach performed a small unhelpful moth.

Because of that, Elise started poking around for truths, not buttons. The town's tiny dusty library smelled of paper and postponed ambitions. Sunlight made a theatre of motes. She ignored the tempting Prophecies of the Peculiar Poodle and looked for pots. Old records, brittle photographs of stern people, and a quiet story: a potter named Agnes, who had made sturdy practical vessels in the town's early days. Water, grain, preserves. No sprites. No giggles. Honest clay and work.

Meanwhile Tibbs, oblivious, created the Festival of the Spritely Tear, flamboyant banners, papier-mâché sprites that resembled grumpy garden gnomes who had lost their hats, and a slightly-too-sweet lemonade called Sprite's Kiss.

Because of that, the townsfolk — generally sensible despite their mayor — noticed discrepancies. Little Timmy O'Malley, whose father baked cakes that needed no mythology, asked, "Mayor Tibbs, if the sprite's tears grant good cheer, why does my tummy rumble after your Sprite Tear cake? It tastes like really sweet lemonade and a bit of disappointment." Old Farmer Giles, who had lived in Willow Creek longer than anyone could remember, grumbled that he had never seen a sprite in his life, and he had seen more critters than the local zoo, and he had had a lot of hot dinners.

A playful rivalry bloomed. Elise quietly shared Agnes: the wheel, the river clay, the pots that had actually held the winter. Tibbs countered with even more outlandish adventures for the vessel, voice like a ship's horn. The tourists, bless them, thought it was all part of the show. They ate it up, including the lemonade.

Until finally, at the grand Festival, with the town gathered and cameras snapping, Mayor Tibbs stood on a makeshift stage, holding the lopsided pot aloft, ready to pour tap water he had labelled Bottled Sprite Tears. Elise's heart did a drum solo she did not enjoy. Whispering in the library would not be enough. She took from her pocket a small smooth stone — a pebble from the actual riverbed, not far from where the pot had been found.

"Mayor Tibbs!" Her voice surprised her by being steady. "Before we pour the sprite's tears, perhaps we should remember the true Willow Creek. This pot was not for mythical sprites. It was for water, from our own river. And this" — she held up the pebble, cool, ordinary — "is from that river. A reminder of where we come from."

The stage wood hummed under Tibbs's unfinished boom. The air smelled of damp earth, slightly burnt hot dogs, and a perfume that was distinctly not tears. From the back, a child giggled, pure and unhelpful to legend. Another joined. Soon the square was full of the real article: laughter that had not been commissioned. Tourists lowered cameras. A woman with kind eyes said, "Oh, this is much better. So authentic. Much more charming than any grumpy gnome."

Ever since then, Elise Porter sold fewer pharaoh's sock drawers and more of what a thing had actually been. She found that a true story, told with a little heart and no sprite, could still empty a suitcase. Mayor Tibbs still put on a show — he was not a man to retire a monocle — but the flourishes now attached themselves to grit: Agnes's kiln, the river, the pot that had held water and not a policy. He may even have started a tour called Willow Creek: Simply Real, which was still, in fairness, a bit of a production. The lopsided pot sat on a library table with a small card, Agnes's name spelled correctly, and Mrs. Higgins, waving from next door, had one new fact worth gossiping, which she did, at length, without once mentioning hair days.
characters: Elise Porter (travelling saleswoman), Mayor Tibbs (heritage entrepreneur)
